common_name: Texas Baby Blue Eyes (Large-Flowered Baby Blue Eyes)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall (September-November) into humus-rich, well-drained soil; the plant overwinters as a low rosette and will not bloom well if sown in spring, much like Texas bluebonnets.

directions: Direct sow seed in fall into humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade to morning sun, covering seed lightly since exposure to light aids germination; like Texas bluebonnets, this native annual establishes as a low rosette over winter and needs the cold season to flower well the following spring. Give it filtered light beneath oaks or along woodland edges and keep soil evenly moist through germination and bloom, then allow it to dry out with summer heat. In March and April the sprawling plants are covered in inch-wide sky-blue flowers with white throats, considerably larger and showier than the related California Baby Blue Eyes, making a soft companion groundcover to bluebonnets and other spring ephemerals. Once established, self-sown seedlings return reliably in the same beds each fall.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring after the last frost, or in fall in mild climates, into lean, well-drained soil; the taproot resents disturbance so sow in place rather than transplanting.

directions: Direct sow seed in spring after the last frost, or in fall in mild climates, into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this taprooted Texas and southern Plains native resents disturbance once established, so sow it where it is to grow rather than transplanting. Slender, wiry stems carry loose spikes of small flowers that open white to soft pink in the evening and blush to deep rose-red as they age, giving the plant a two-toned look on the same stem. It tolerates heat, drought, and poor caliche soils far better than rich garden ground, and works well in native meadow plantings, pollinator gardens, or rock gardens where its airy, see-through habit can mix with bunchgrasses. Deadheading extends bloom from late spring into fall, though plants also self-seed readily if spent flower spikes are left in place.

common_name: Horse Crippler (Devil's Head Cactus, Candy Cactus)

planting.note: Start seed indoors in sterile, gritty cactus mix, or set out nursery-grown plants in spring into rocky, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Start seed indoors in a sterile, gritty cactus mix under warm conditions, or set out nursery-grown plants in spring into rocky, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; this low, flattened, ground-hugging cactus of Texas and the southern Plains is nearly stemless and easy to overlook in short grass until its stout, strongly recurved spines catch an ankle or a horse's hoof, the source of its common name. Bright pink to magenta cup-shaped flowers appear at the crown in late spring, followed by fleshy red fruit that was historically candied by early Texas settlers. Because it lacks offsets and grows very slowly, propagation is almost always from seed, and mature specimens take many years to reach flowering size and should be left undisturbed once sited. It is exceptionally drought and heat tolerant and needs no supplemental water once established, suiting rock gardens and xeric plantings that mimic native prairie and caliche soils.

common_name: Texas Barrel Cactus (Turk's Head Cactus, Glory of Texas)

planting.note: Start seed indoors in warm, sterile mineral cactus mix, or transplant nursery stock in spring into sharply drained, gravelly or caliche soil in full sun.

directions: Start seed indoors in warm, sterile mineral cactus mix, or transplant nursery stock in spring into sharply drained, gravelly or caliche soil in full sun; native to the Rio Grande Plains of South Texas and adjacent Mexico, this ribbed, cylindrical barrel cactus is armed with stout, strongly hooked central spines for which it is named. Bright yellow flowers with a reddish throat open at the crown in summer, followed by fleshy yellow fruit, and older solitary stems can eventually reach two feet or more in height over many years. It is somewhat less cold hardy than the more northern Ferocactus wislizeni, so in the coolest parts of its recommended zones a covered or south-facing site helps protect it from prolonged hard freezes. Water only sparingly during the growing season and keep it essentially dry over winter, as this species is highly susceptible to rot in wet or poorly draining soil.

planting.note: Start seed indoors in a lean, sterile cactus mix, or plant offsets in spring into rocky, well-drained soil in full sun; extremely cold hardy compared to most cacti.

directions: Start seed indoors in a lean, sterile cactus mix, or plant offsets in spring into rocky, well-drained soil in full sun; this small, densely spined, clustering cactus ranges from the southern Canadian prairies through the Great Plains into the Texas Panhandle and Trans-Pecos, making it one of the most cold-hardy cacti native to North America. Globe-shaped stems bear a starburst pattern of radiating spines and slowly form tight clumps of a dozen or more heads, topped in late spring by bright pink to magenta flowers followed by small green fruit that ripens the following year. Because it thrives on neglect and rots quickly in heavy or poorly drained soil, plant it in a raised bed or scree garden of coarse gravel and mineral soil and water only during active summer growth. Its extreme cold tolerance makes it a good choice for xeric rock gardens well outside the range of most other ornamental cacti.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Little Nipple Cactus (Corky-Seed Cactus, Nipple Beehive Cactus)

planting.note: Start seed indoors in a sterile, gritty cactus mix, or set out nursery-grown plants in spring into rocky, alkaline, sharply drained soil in full sun.

directions: Start seed indoors in a sterile, gritty cactus mix under warm conditions, or set out nursery-grown plants in spring into rocky, alkaline, sharply drained soil in full sun; native to south and central Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and northern Mexico, this low, often solitary globose cactus grows nearly flush with the ground and is easy to overlook until its ring of small white to pink flowers opens around the crown in spring. Showy club-shaped red-pink fruits follow later in the year and persist for months, adding color long after bloom has finished. The plant's small size and slow growth make it well suited to rock gardens, trough plantings, and gravel beds where it can be viewed up close, and it needs no supplemental water once established in appropriately gritty soil. Avoid rich or moisture-retentive soils, which quickly lead to rot in this drought-adapted species.

common_name: Star Cactus (Sand Dollar Cactus, Sea Urchin Cactus)

planting.note: Start seed indoors in warm, humid conditions over a sterile mineral cactus mix; always source nursery-propagated seed or plants since wild populations are federally endangered.

directions: Start seed indoors in warm, humid conditions over a sterile mineral cactus mix, since this species germinates readily from seed but rarely produces offsets; native to a small area of extreme South Texas and adjacent Mexico, it is federally listed as endangered in the wild, and plants in cultivation should always be nursery-propagated from seed rather than collected. The flattened, spineless, globose stem is divided into broad ribs dotted with small tufts of white wool, giving it a distinctive sand-dollar or sea-urchin appearance unlike any spined cactus. Large yellow flowers with a red-orange throat open at the crown in warm weather, often repeating over several weeks. Because it is less cold hardy than most Texas native cacti, grow it in a very gritty, fast-draining mix in full sun to light shade and bring container plants under cover or into a greenhouse whenever hard freezes threaten.
